n: After seven days of silence, Job finally speaks — and he curses the day he was born. Notice he does not curse God, as Satan predicted; he curses his own birthday.

f.g: Cursed his birthday, not God.

n: From here until chapter 42 the book shifts from prose story to Hebrew poetry. Job’s raw, honest lament begins.

f.g: Literally “answered” — responding to his situation.

n: Job wishes the day of his birth — and the night he was conceived — had never existed. The two lines use Hebrew parallelism: saying the same idea twice in different words.

f.g: A boy is conceived — announcing the start of his life.

n: He wishes that day would be wrapped in darkness, as if reversing God’s first creative word, “Let there be light.”

f.g: A reversal of Genesis 1:3, “Let there be light.”
Pay attention to, care about.

n: He piles up images of gloom — deep darkness, clouds, eclipse — hoping to blot that day out entirely.

f.g: Deep darkness, the thickest gloom (compare Psalms 23:4).
Literally “redeem” or “claim it back” — let darkness take it back.

n: Let that night be erased from the calendar, never counted among the days of the year.

f.w: let it not be joined unto the days of the year
f.g: Let it be removed from the calendar.

n: Let that night be barren and silent, with no joyful birth cry or celebration.

f.g: Barren, empty.

n: Job calls on those skilled in cursing — even those who can rouse the sea monster Leviathan — to curse that day. He uses ancient imagery of chaos.

f.g: The Hebrew reads “Leviathan,” a mythic sea monster symbolizing chaos (Job 41:1; Isaiah 27:1).

n: Let that night’s morning stars stay dark, waiting for a dawn that never comes.

f.g: Literally “the eyelids of the morning” — the first rays of dawn.

n: Why curse that day? Because it didn’t keep him from being born and seeing such sorrow.

f.w: shut not up the doors of my mother's womb
f.g: Didn’t prevent his birth.

n: Now Job asks “why?” — the first of many questions in the book. Why didn’t I die at birth?

f.g: Die, breathe my last.

n: Why was I received onto my mother’s knees and nursed? Why was I cared for at all?

f.g: In KJV English, “come before, receive” — the knees that received him at birth.

n: If he had died, he would now be resting peacefully. Job imagines death as quiet sleep, an escape from pain.

f.g: Death is often pictured as sleep in scripture (Daniel 12:2).

n: He would be resting with the kings and advisers of the past, whose grand buildings have now fallen into ruin. Death levels all human greatness.

f.g: Built monuments or tombs that now lie in ruins.

n: Or with wealthy princes whose silver-filled houses could not keep them from death.
Or he could have been like a stillborn child, never seeing the light of life at all.

f.g: A miscarried or stillborn baby.

n: In the grave, the wicked can no longer cause trouble, and the exhausted find rest. Job longs for that peace.

f.w: there the weary be at rest

n: Prisoners there are at ease, no longer hearing the shouts of their slave drivers.

f.g: The shout of the taskmaster.

n: In death, small and great are equal, and the slave is free from his master. Job sees death as a great equalizer.

f.w: The small and great are there

n: Job widens his question: why does God give life to people who only suffer? It is the cry of countless sufferers through history.

f.g: Deeply anguished.

n: They long for death, searching for it more eagerly than for buried treasure, yet it doesn’t come.

f.w: dig for it more than for hid treasures

n: They would rejoice to find the grave. This shows the depth of Job’s despair — honest feelings the book does not hide.

f.w: when they can find the grave
f.g: When they finally die.

n: Why give life to someone who can’t see a way forward, whom God has fenced in? Ironically, Satan had complained God put a protective hedge around Job; now Job feels hemmed in.

f.g: Who cannot see the path ahead.

n: His groans come in place of food, and his cries pour out like water.

f.w: my sighing cometh before I eat
f.g: Groaning has become his daily bread.
Loud groans of anguish (Psalms 22:1).

n: The very thing he feared most has happened. Even in prosperity, Job may have worried about losing it all — and now he has.

f.w: the thing which I greatly feared
f.g: His worst fears have come true.

n: He has no peace, no quiet, no rest — only trouble. The chapter ends without resolution, setting up the long debate with his friends.

f.g: Literally “turmoil came” — the same word used for anger or agitation.
